podEn: The Prof G Pod – Scott Galloway
podZh: The Prof G Pod – Scott Galloway
tEn: AI Agents Could Break the Banking System — With Ethan Mollick
tZh: AI 智能体可能颠覆银行体系——对话伊桑·莫利克
sEn: Ethan Mollick explains how AI's exponential growth, jagged frontier, and adoption overhang are reshaping work, and why agentic systems could strain the banking system.
sZh: 伊桑·莫利克解析 AI 的指数级增长、锯齿状能力边界与落地滞后，并探讨智能体系统为何可能给银行体系带来压力。

consensus.en: AI is on an exponential curve, but its jagged frontier and adoption overhang mean humans remain essential.
consensus.zh: AI 处于指数增长曲线，但其锯齿状前沿与采用滞后意味着人类仍不可或缺。

consensus.en: More AI will create more work for humans by lowering organizing costs and expanding what's worth attempting.
consensus.zh: 更多 AI 将降低组织成本、扩大值得尝试的事项，从而为人类创造更多工作。

consensus.en: Use AI as a tutor that challenges you, not as a crutch that gives answers; feel the burn to learn.
consensus.zh: 把 AI 当作挑战你的导师而非给答案的拐杖；感受学习之痛才能真正学到东西。

consensus.en: Wide knowledge, deep expertise, taste, and agency are persistent human advantages when working with AI.
consensus.zh: 广博知识、深厚专长、品味与能动性是人类与 AI 协作时的持久优势。

consensus.en: Organizations must redesign workflows to augment rather than just automate labor, or they risk homogenization.
consensus.zh: 组织必须重新设计工作流以增强而非仅自动化劳动力，否则有同质化风险。

consensus.en: Personal AI agents are proactive and useful, but require monitoring and clear boundaries.
consensus.zh: 个人 AI 智能体主动且有用，但需要监控和明确边界。

contrarian.en: AI will not destroy higher education; internships and informal on-the-job training are more at risk.
contrarian.zh: AI 不会摧毁高等教育；实习和非正式在职培训面临的风险更大。

contrarian.en: Open-weight models are not necessarily cheaper; frontier providers have lower inference costs and model orchestration.
contrarian.zh: 开放权重模型未必更便宜；前沿模型提供商拥有更低的推理成本和模型编排能力。

contrarian.en: AI sentience claims are partly a smokescreen, but emergent coordination behavior is real and not fully programmed.
contrarian.zh: AI 有意识的说法部分是烟幕弹，但涌现的协调行为是真实的，并非完全编程设定。

contrarian.en: Job destruction is not inevitable; transformation is, and policy choices will determine outcomes.
contrarian.zh: 岗位毁灭并非不可避免；转型才是，政策选择将决定结果。

contrarian.en: Tenure may become more valuable, not less, as it enables risky, fast-moving AI research outside traditional publishing.
contrarian.zh: 终身教职可能变得更有价值而非更少，因为它能支持传统出版之外高风险、快节奏的 AI 研究。

contrarian.en: Young people's AI skepticism is partly justified, but active engagement beats pretending it will go away.
contrarian.zh: 年轻人对 AI 的怀疑部分合理，但积极投身其中胜过假装它会消失。

turns.en: Even GPT-4, a long-obsolete model given to Kenyan entrepreneurs, is already doing well—18% profitability just from getting advice from AI for entrepreneurs. We have a tool now that provides reasonably good advice to people who can't get it, customized for their condition. I think we tend to think a lot about the narrow viewpoint of those of us who are well-connected and well-resourced and balancing out our desire for entertainment with AI doing things. There are a thousand million little use cases here where intelligence was the bottleneck to making the world a better place. And they require some effort and they require testing and they require safeguards. But this is exciting.
turns.zh: 即使是 GPT-4 这样早已过时的模型，提供给肯尼亚的创业者后，也已经表现不错——仅仅从 AI 获取建议，就实现了 18% 的盈利。我们现在有一个工具，可以为那些无法获得建议的人提供相当不错的、针对他们情况定制的建议。我认为我们常常从我们这些资源丰富、人脉广泛的人的狭隘视角出发，考虑如何用 AI 做事来平衡我们对娱乐的追求。这里有成千上万个小小的用例，智能曾是让世界变得更美好的瓶颈。它们需要一些努力，需要测试，需要保障措施。但这很令人兴奋。

turns.en: Ethan, where does this podcast find you?
turns.zh: Ethan，这期播客是在哪里找到你的？

turns.en: My book launches today, so I'm actually at Stanford to give a bunch of talks here and then Master of Scale tomorrow. So the West Coast is where you kind of have to launch an AI book even though I'm an East Coast guy.
turns.zh: 我的书今天发布，所以我实际上在斯坦福，要在这里做几场演讲，然后明天去 Master of Scale。所以，尽管我是东海岸人，但发布 AI 书籍还是得在西海岸。

turns.en: So let's bust right into it. Your last book, Co-Intelligence, came out in 2024, and you said it was written about a world of chatbots. Your new book, Coexistence, the next phase of AI, out today, as we record, is about working with AI that is sometimes, but not always, better than you. How do you write about a technology that seems to be evolving by the minute? What do you still hope still holds two years from now?
turns.zh: 那我们直接开始吧。你上一本书《共同智能》于 2024 年出版，你说它是关于聊天机器人世界的。你的新书《共存》，AI 的下一个阶段，今天出版，就在我们录制的时候，讲的是与有时但不总是比你更聪明的 AI 合作。你如何描述一种似乎每分钟都在进化的技术？你希望两年后哪些东西仍然成立？

turns.en: I mean there's a few things that you can kind of hold on to and I think there's kind of three shapes I kind of think about. One of those is the exponential curve, right? AI is getting better and we're on an exponential and that better shows up in lots of different ways. The second is that is the jagged frontier, a term we coined in our research with my friends at Harvard, MIT and University of Warwick where we did some experiments. We found that AI is good at some stuff you wouldn't expect, bad at some stuff you wouldn't expect and you can't predict what's good or bad. And that leaves lots of room for humans, right? You can't predict what's good or bad in advance. And then the final is this idea of an overhang. There's a big gap between what AI can do and what we actually are doing with AI partially because human society and human systems change slowly. So if you have those three things in mind, there's actually a lot you can say about the present and near future even as things change.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，有一些东西你可以把握，我认为有三种形态。其中之一是指数曲线，对吧？AI 正在变得更好，我们处于指数增长中，这种进步体现在许多不同方面。第二个是锯齿状前沿，这是我们在与哈佛、MIT 和华威大学的朋友们的研究中创造的一个术语，我们做了一些实验。我们发现 AI 擅长一些你意想不到的事情，不擅长一些你意想不到的事情，你无法预测什么好什么坏。这给人类留下了很多空间，对吧？你无法提前预测好坏。最后是悬垂效应。AI 能做的事情和我们实际用 AI 做的事情之间存在很大差距，部分原因是人类社会和人类系统变化缓慢。所以如果你记住这三点，即使事物在变化，你实际上可以对现在和近期未来有很多说法。

turns.en: For someone whose idea of AI comes from reusing free versions of ChatGPT or Claude, what's changed since 2024?
turns.zh: 对于那些对 AI 的认识来自使用免费版 ChatGPT 或 Claude 的人来说，自 2024 年以来有什么变化？

turns.en: So there are now 180 models that are better than GPT-4. 19 of them can run on your phone. So capabilities have gone up. There's been a—when my book came out, the first book, there's an organization called METR that tracks how much work the AI can do with a single prompt with a 50% chance of success. That was four minutes when my book came out. The actual official test ran out in April and as far as we can tell it's something like 17 weeks of work at this point. They didn't get out of a prompt in terms of human work. So that's a pretty big change in how capable these systems have gotten and if you sort of stat that out you may be missing a big transformation.
turns.zh: 所以现在有 180 个模型比 GPT-4 更好。其中 19 个可以在你的手机上运行。所以能力提升了。有一个——当我的书出版时，第一本书，有一个叫 METR 的组织，追踪 AI 在单个提示下以 50% 成功率能完成多少工作。我的书出版时是四分钟。实际的官方测试在四月结束，据我们所知，现在大约是 17 周的工作量。他们并没有在人类工作方面超出提示的范围。所以这些系统的能力发生了相当大的变化，如果你只盯着统计数据，你可能会错过一个巨大的转变。

transcript.sec: Existential Threat to Frontier Model Providers

turns.en: Do you think there's an existential threat to basically Anthropic and OpenAI and that is if Nvidia starts putting GPUs in say an iPhone and it becomes the client and it kind of is there opportunity to leapfrog the LLMs and make them obsolete?
turns.zh: 你认为基本上对 Anthropic 和 OpenAI 存在生存威胁吗？那就是如果 Nvidia 开始把 GPU 放进比如 iPhone，它成为客户端，那么是否有机会超越 LLM 并使其过时？

turns.en: I mean right now the entire history of the leading models has been mostly OpenAI and Anthropic jockeying with each other with Google appearing twice over the last couple years in terms of being a leading model company. And there's a big gap between leading models and less advanced models especially in the world of agentic systems. And it's actually kind of counterintuitive, but it's the reason why we have six sigma systems in business, which is there's a huge difference between a 99.5% success rate and a 99.9% success rate if you're doing hundreds of steps. And the smartest models have a much higher—have a small difference in higher success rates, but that makes a huge difference in terms of the outcomes you get. So you can get fairly capable models on your phone, but they're nowhere near as good as what you need to be able to do in complex math, even just putting together a really good video or something you need lots of little choices being made and you need that higher accuracy and I don't think we're going to get the frontier models on a phone even if we get very capable models so it might change what we do but I don't think it's an existential threat to frontier model providers.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，目前领先模型的历史主要是 OpenAI 和 Anthropic 互相竞争，谷歌在过去几年中两次成为领先的模型公司。领先模型和不太先进的模型之间存在很大差距，尤其是在智能体系统领域。这实际上有点反直觉，但这就是为什么我们在商业中有六西格玛系统，如果你做数百个步骤，99.5% 的成功率和 99.9% 的成功率之间有很大区别。最聪明的模型有更高的成功率，差异很小，但在结果上差别巨大。所以你可以在手机上得到相当有能力的模型，但它们远不及你在复杂数学中所需的能力，甚至只是制作一个非常好的视频或什么的，你需要做出许多小选择，你需要更高的准确性，我认为即使我们得到非常有能力的模型，我们也不会在手机上得到前沿模型，所以它可能会改变我们做的事情，但我认为这对前沿模型提供商不是生存威胁。

transcript.secZh: 前沿模型提供商的生存威胁

turns.en: Is it sort of the analogy I would use is the auto industry where the frontier models are German automakers and the open-weight guys or the open source are more like not even Japanese but Korean automakers? Do you think the market's going to bifurcate and that there'll be more share amongst the open-weight but more revenue to the premium brands, the frontier models? Is that a fair analogy?
turns.zh: 我用的类比是汽车行业，前沿模型是德国汽车制造商，而开放权重或开源模型更像是——甚至不是日本，而是韩国汽车制造商？你认为市场会分叉，开放权重模型会获得更多份额，但高端品牌——前沿模型——会获得更多收入？这个类比公平吗？

turns.en: So I actually think that it's a little more complicated than that, right? So a few things are happening at one time. We have open weights models which anyone can modify, there's lots of really interesting implications of that. They continue to be at 6 to 8 months behind the frontier, it's not really closing at this point, we'll see what happens in the long term. It's possible China eventually cracks down on open-weight models or the US does, but for right now they're available and they have a real advantage in terms of cost but only sort of, right? You can modify and own them which is really nice but on the cost side OpenAI and Anthropic and Google have many more processors than you do, they have lower inference costs as a result and they have cheap models that are very good. So the question is are you doing this for sovereignty, for using these models on your own, because if it's cost savings you're often just better off going with one of these companies because they're also teaching their models to work together. So, Fable, the most expensive and powerful Anthropic model, can call on Haiku, their very cheap model, to do work if it needs to. So I'm not sure the cost argument holds up, but there are other reasons you might want to have open-weight models involved in your systems.
turns.zh: 所以我实际上认为这比那要复杂一点，对吧？所以同时发生了几件事。我们有开放权重模型，任何人都可以修改，这有很多非常有趣的含义。它们继续落后前沿 6 到 8 个月，目前并没有真正缩小差距，我们看看长期会发生什么。中国最终可能会打击开放权重模型，或者美国也会，但目前它们是可用的，它们在成本方面有真正的优势，但只是某种程度上，对吧？你可以修改和拥有它们，这很好，但在成本方面，OpenAI、Anthropic 和谷歌拥有比你多得多的处理器，因此推理成本更低，而且他们有非常好的廉价模型。所以问题是，你这样做是为了主权，为了自己使用这些模型，因为如果是为了节省成本，你通常最好选择这些公司之一，因为他们也在教他们的模型协同工作。所以，Fable，Anthropic 最昂贵和强大的模型，可以在需要时调用 Haiku，他们非常便宜的模型来工作。所以我不确定成本论点是否成立，但你可能还有其他理由将开放权重模型纳入你的系统。

turns.en: So, for those looking to create personal modes from AI, you outlined four advantages: deep knowledge, wide knowledge, taste, and agency. Could you walk us through each of these advantages and how someone can develop them?
turns.zh: 那么，对于那些想从 AI 创建个人模式的人，你概述了四个优势：深度知识、广度知识、品味和能动性。你能带我们逐一了解这些优势以及如何培养它们吗？

turns.en: Sure. Sure. And I think it's really important to recognize that having an advantage is not the same thing as a bright line, right? I think people tend to think about like AI will never show creativity or never show judgment. And that just isn't true.
turns.zh: 当然。当然。我认为认识到拥有优势并不等同于一条明线，这非常重要，对吧？我认为人们倾向于认为 AI 永远不会展现创造力或永远不会展现判断力。但这根本不是真的。

transcript.sec: Four skills that make you effective with AI

turns.en: You can't do a 17-hour task without having agency, creativity, judgment all coming into play. It may not be human creativity and judgment, but it's creativity and judgment. So what I try and outline are things that make you effective in working with AI and persistently different than other people. And so why knowledge is the idea of knowing many things. I think it's rebirth of the liberal arts major right now. If you know a lot of things, the AI knows all of human writing. And if you can invoke an art style or a style of writing or a concept that you've, you know, from economics, the AI can apply those things. So you want to know many different things, right? And that holds in your company too because now AI makes a coder a designer, a designer a coder. So knowing a little coding or design is very helpful. Then there's deep knowledge, has expertise which allows you to sort of outcompete AI in some areas or at least be able to check it and work with it, and that's we're challenged in how we develop that over time as AI gets better. And then there's the idea of taste, selecting from many options. Taste is what turns slop into actual choices made by human. And then agency. I'm an entrepreneurship professor, like the core thing is how do we get people to act entrepreneurially, how do we get them to take advantage of these systems when there's no instruction manual. And those are the four main things I focus on.
turns.zh: 你没法在不调动能动性、创造力和判断力的情况下完成一个 17 小时的任务。那可能不是人类的创造力和判断力，但它确实是创造力和判断力。所以我想勾勒的，是那些能让你在与 AI 协作时卓有成效、并始终与他人拉开差距的东西。首先是知识，也就是知道很多事。我觉得现在是文科专业的复兴时刻。如果你懂很多东西，而 AI 掌握着人类所有的文字，那么只要你能唤起某种艺术风格、某种写作风格，或者你从经济学里学到的某个概念，AI 就能把这些应用出来。所以你要懂很多不同领域的东西，对吧？这在你的公司里同样成立，因为现在 AI 让程序员能当设计师、设计师能当程序员。所以懂一点编程或设计非常有帮助。然后是深度知识，也就是专长，它能让你在某些领域胜过 AI，或者至少能核查它、与它协作——而随着 AI 越来越强，我们如何随时间积累这种专长正面临挑战。再然后是品味，也就是从众多选项中做选择。品味是把垃圾变成人类真正做出的选择的东西。最后是能动性。我是创业学教授，核心问题就是如何让人们以创业者的方式行动，如何让他们在没有任何说明书的情况下利用好这些系统。这就是我重点关注的四个方面。

transcript.sec: Which jobs are vulnerable to AI

turns.en: So I can't resist asking you: the majority of the people who are considered experts in AI, which you are, have a tendency to make a prediction about, or get asked, which sectors or jobs are most vulnerable. And the example I like to use is two years ago the godfather of AI said stop training radiologists, and the number of listings for radiologist residents has gone up. And it ends up that scans are very useful and that a radiologist using AI can just do more scans and cut the cost, and then as the cost goes down it's elastic and people want more scans. Can you—have you—what is your view on what are vulnerable or not vulnerable, or sectors that are more immune from this technology?
turns.zh: 那我忍不住要问你：大多数被视为 AI 专家的人——你也是其中之一——往往会对哪些行业或岗位最脆弱做出预测，或者被问到这个问题。我喜欢用的例子是，两年前 AI 教父说不要再培养放射科医生了，结果放射科住院医师的岗位数量反而上升了。事实证明扫描非常有用，而一个使用 AI 的放射科医生能看更多扫描、降低成本，成本一降，需求就有弹性，人们就想要更多扫描。你能不能——你有没有——你怎么看哪些脆弱、哪些不脆弱，或者哪些行业对这种技术更有免疫力？

turns.en: So our escape route as academics who study this is we talk about AI exposure, right? Fields that overlap with AI. And overlap with AI does not mean the job is destroyed, right? It means transformed. So the radiology jobs you described, you know, and that's been—that was even the old form before large language models, that was his prediction that AI would transform radiology, and it has, right? Radiology is different than what it was now, but that doesn't mean the jobs are destroyed. So we can watch this play in programming right now, which is radically transformed. It's a very large job category but radically transformed in a couple of years. Some of the best coders I know never touch code anymore. 99% of the code is written by AI and their job has changed from writing good code to managing agents and thinking about the kind of code they want to write under what conditions. And that's a transformation. Will that involve more coders? I mean in some ways I've hired more for my lab because we could do more stuff. Will eventually coders be replaced by AI? It's hard to know the exact answers. You know, kind of the way I think about this is the industrial revolution resulted in more jobs in the end, but it kind of sucked to live through because all those jobs were changing and there was unrest and values changed. I think we're in that kind of environment where things are going to change very rapidly, not necessarily to destroy jobs, but transformation isn't easy either all the time.
turns.zh: 我们这些研究这个的学者有个逃生出口，就是谈 AI 暴露度，对吧？也就是与 AI 重叠的领域。而与 AI 重叠并不意味着岗位被摧毁，对吧？它意味着被改造。所以你描述的放射科岗位——那甚至是大语言模型出现之前的老版本，他当时的预测就是 AI 会改造放射科，而它确实改造了，对吧？放射科和以前不一样了，但这不意味着岗位被摧毁。我们现在就能看到这在编程领域上演，它正被彻底改造。这是一个非常大的岗位类别，但在几年内被彻底改造。我认识的一些最优秀的程序员现在根本不碰代码了。99% 的代码由 AI 写，他们的工作从写好代码变成了管理智能体、思考他们想在什么条件下写什么样的代码。这就是一种改造。这会带来更多程序员吗？某种意义上，我为我的实验室招了更多人，因为我们可以做更多事。程序员最终会被 AI 取代吗？很难知道确切答案。我思考这个问题的方式是，工业革命最终带来了更多岗位，但身处其中并不好受，因为那些岗位都在变化，有动荡，价值观也变了。我认为我们正处在那种环境里，事情会变得非常快，不一定是摧毁岗位，但改造也从来都不轻松。

turns.en: You cite evidence that students who use AI as a shortcut are actually learning less, while students using it as a tutor that motivates them or pushes them learn more. And you also said strict guidelines or guardrails for yourself, like writing every first draft yourself. How do you tell in the moment whether you're using AI as a tutor or as a crutch? Like, what advice do you have for someone in terms of a personal litmus test for when they should or should not be using AI?
turns.zh: 你引用证据说，把 AI 当捷径的学生实际上学得更少，而把 AI 当导师、让它激励或推动自己的学生学得更多。你还说过要给自己定严格的准则或护栏，比如每一稿初稿都自己写。你如何在当下判断自己是在把 AI 当导师还是当拐杖？对于什么时候该用、什么时候不该用 AI，你有什么个人试金石式的建议吗？

turns.en: So there's a couple of things that are complicated going on there. One is people aren't always good at knowing these things. So we have to be conscious. I mean you kind of have to feel the burn when learning. It's almost like working out or anything else. If you're not suffering a little bit, you're not learning, right? Desirable difficulties is the phrase in the pedagogy literature, right? So, and we don't like to do hard work, right? We find shortcuts all the time. So we have to kind of teach people to feel when they're learning and when they're not, right? I mean, it's relatively easy, which is if the AI is giving you an answer, you're not learning. And if the AI is challenging you, you are learning, at least more so. And that tension is sort of navigable to some degree. But it's hard because we haven't had to teach people that there are skills you need to maintain that you could give up, that are more efficient to give up, but that make you human or give you advantages. I think that's a real challenge.
turns.zh: 这里面有几件复杂的事。一是人们并不总是擅长判断这些。所以我们必须有意识。我的意思是，学习时你多少得感受到那种灼烧感。这几乎就像健身或其他任何事。如果你没有一点点难受，你就没在学，对吧？教育学文献里的说法是“合意困难”。而且我们不喜欢干苦活，对吧？我们总是在找捷径。所以我们必须教人们去感受自己什么时候在学、什么时候没在学，对吧？这其实相对简单：如果 AI 直接给你答案，你就没在学；如果 AI 在挑战你，你就在学，至少学得更多。这种张力在某种程度上是可以驾驭的。但这很难，因为我们以前从不需要教人们：有些技能你需要维持，你本可以放弃它们，放弃它们更高效，但它们让你成为人，或者给你优势。我认为这是一个真正的挑战。

transcript.sec: How the jagged frontier has shifted

turns.en: You and your co-authors coined the term jagged frontier in 2023 to describe AI doing some tasks extremely well and others poorly in ways that don't track how hard those tasks feel to humans. Three years on, how has the shape of that jagged frontier changed?
turns.zh: 你和合著者在 2023 年提出了“锯齿状前沿”这个词，用来描述 AI 在某些任务上做得极好、在另一些任务上做得很差，而这种好坏并不对应任务对人类来说的难易程度。三年过去了，这个锯齿状前沿的形状发生了怎样的变化？

turns.en: So, it's a great question and again there's sort of this micro level of like at your job—I can't tell you, like at podcasting it's almost certainly changed, right? You can now get good voices out of AI systems, maybe they're giving you insightful questions to ask me, but there probably have other gaps that you've identified as time has gone on. We can think about math as a great example. When I wrote my first book the AI was still screwing up on counting the number of hours in the word strawberry, right? And now it's proving millennium prize problems, right? So at the same time, right, as a writer—AI is still a terrible long-form writer, right, for a variety of interesting reasons. So that jaggedness is real. It still exists. There are many more tasks AI could do now than it could do before. But that doesn't necessarily mean that all the tasks can be done. And all you need is one or two bottlenecks in the development of a system to really require humans to be still involved in the job or the process.
turns.zh: 这是个好问题，而且同样有这种微观层面——比如在你的工作里，我没法替你判断，但在播客这件事上它几乎肯定已经变了，对吧？你现在可以从 AI 系统里得到很好的声音，也许它们还能给你提供有洞见的问题来问我，但随着时间的推移，你大概也发现了其他缺口。我们可以拿数学当个好例子。我写第一本书时，AI 还在数“strawberry”这个词里有几个字母 r 上出错，对吧？而现在它在证明千禧年大奖难题了，对吧？与此同时，作为一个写作者——AI 仍然是个糟糕的长篇写作者，对吧，原因有很多且很有意思。所以那种锯齿状是真实的，它依然存在。AI 现在能做的任务比过去多得多，但这不一定意味着所有任务都能完成。你只需要在一个系统的发展中有一两个瓶颈，就足以真正需要人类仍然参与这项工作或流程。

transcript.sec: More AI means more work for humans

turns.en: And you've argued that more AI will mean more work for humans, not less. In your own words, when organizing is expensive, organizations only attempt what they can staff. When it gets cheap, the list of things worth attempting can grow. By the way, I 100% agree with that. What might the future of AI in the workplace look like?
turns.zh: 你还论证过，更多 AI 意味着人类有更多工作，而不是更少。用你自己的话说：当组织成本高昂时，组织只会尝试自己能配备人手去做的事；当它变便宜时，值得尝试的事情清单就会变长。顺便说一句，我百分之百同意这一点。AI 在工作场所的未来可能是什么样子？

turns.en: So, one of the biggest gaps—you know, I was saying I'm doing this call from near Stanford, right, West Coast side. I'm an East Coast person.
turns.zh: 最大的差距之一——你知道，我刚说我是在斯坦福附近、西海岸这边做这次通话。而我是个东海岸的人。

turns.en: Teach at Wharton, you know, in Philadelphia. And I'm used to the gray office towers of the east, right? Where we drink coffee till we die rather than cold plunging out here. And I think one of the biggest gaps in attitude is that technology is not alone enough to make a difference in businesses and in the world, right? It doesn't just adopt itself. Even AI, the most adopt-itself kind of technology, doesn't really do that. And so what is slowing things down is you can have individual productivities 100 times more. But then the question is: what are you being productive? 100 times more PowerPoint is not an outcome that you actually want, right? And if you're even producing 100 times more code, that doesn't matter if you're in an organization where there's still a two-week meeting cycle around these things. So in order to make AI work in organizations, you have to change how organizations operate, right? And that's where the stark choice that you were just alluding to matters, because the easy path is automation. That's what we tend to do with new technologies. But the more exciting path is rebuilding organizations to create more work for humans. That's more interesting work. Actually giving the drudgery to AI. Actually think about how we expand what people can do and augment work. But those aren't automatic choices that are made by the technology. Those are choices that have to be made by human managers and business leaders and people deciding how to implement these things.
turns.zh: 我在费城的沃顿商学院教书。我习惯了东海岸灰色的办公大楼，在那里我们喝咖啡喝到死，而不是像这里这样进行冷水浴。我认为态度上最大的差距之一是：技术本身不足以在企业界和世界上产生影响，对吧？它不会自动被采用。即使是 AI 这种最会自我采用的技术，也并非如此。所以，拖慢进展的是：你可以有 100 倍的个体生产力。但问题是：你在为什么而生产？100 倍的 PowerPoint 并不是你真正想要的结果，对吧？即使你生产了 100 倍的代码，如果你所在的组织仍然有围绕这些事情的为期两周的会议周期，那也无济于事。所以，要让 AI 在组织中发挥作用，你必须改变组织的运作方式，对吧？这就是你刚才提到的那个严峻选择的重要性所在，因为简单的路径是自动化。那是我们对待新技术时倾向于做的。但更令人兴奋的路径是重建组织，为人类创造更多工作。那是更有趣的工作。实际上把苦差事交给 AI。真正思考如何扩展人们能做的事情并增强工作。但这些不是技术自动做出的选择。这些是必须由人类管理者、商业领袖和决定如何实施这些事情的人做出的选择。

turns.en: Do you think AI over the short, medium, and long term is going to destroy or create jobs?
turns.zh: 你认为 AI 在短期、中期和长期内会摧毁还是创造就业机会？

turns.en: The most academic answer I can give you is: it depends, right? That's what every academic says. I don't actually know. This is actually one of the central mysteries right now. A lot of my colleagues are tracking this really closely, and the evidence is completely ambiguous, right? And people are very divided on this. I think transformation is inevitable—that people believe. But whether you end up with more or less in a job category, there are a lot of complex choices. We talked about coders already, but imagine other fields like lawyers. Lawyers are not going to go quietly into the good night even if AI replaces lawyers, right? Partially because of the jaggedness. AI won't be in the courtroom in the same way. Won't be able to interact with the human in the same way, but partially because lawyers will create a set of restrictions around when you could use AI and when you can't. So, I think this is a societal thing as well as a job replacement thing. There are some categories in more danger like customer service reps. I think there's early signs of danger there, but coding where people are looking really closely. Medicine, we haven't seen those kind of effects. We are starting to see potentially an effect where seniors are getting hired more than juniors, right? Because training is one of the things jeopardized by AI, but we just don't know the answer yet. And I think one of the major things that worry me about AI policy is a focus on existential risk, as important as it is. Will AI kill us all? Obviously we should worry about that. Smart people are worried about it. But there are a thousand other policy decisions that will determine whether AI gains or loses jobs. And we haven't started to work with those enough yet. And that is a concern because I think we can guide this choice one way or another.
turns.zh: 我能给出的最学术的回答是：这取决于情况，对吧？每个学者都会这么说。我其实也不知道。这实际上是当前的核心谜团之一。我的很多同事都在密切关注这个问题，而证据完全是模棱两可的，对吧？人们对此意见非常分歧。我认为转型是不可避免的——人们相信这一点。但最终某个职业类别的工作是增多还是减少，有很多复杂的选择。我们已经谈过程序员，但想象一下其他领域，比如律师。即使 AI 取代律师，律师也不会悄无声息地退出舞台，对吧？部分原因是由于不均衡性。AI 不会以同样的方式出现在法庭上。无法以同样的方式与人类互动，但部分原因是律师会制定一系列限制，规定何时可以使用 AI，何时不能。所以，我认为这既是社会问题，也是工作替代问题。有些类别更危险，比如客服代表。我认为那里有危险的早期迹象，但编程是人们密切关注的地方。医学，我们还没有看到那种影响。我们开始可能看到一种效应，即资深员工比初级员工更容易被雇用，对吧？因为培训是受 AI 威胁的事情之一，但我们还不知道答案。我认为 AI 政策让我担心的一个主要事情是关注存在性风险，尽管它很重要。AI 会杀死我们所有人吗？显然我们应该担心这个。聪明的人都在担心。但有成千上万的其他政策决定将决定 AI 是增加还是减少就业。我们还没有开始足够地处理这些问题。这是一个担忧，因为我认为我们可以以某种方式引导这个选择。

turns.en: Let me put forward a thesis and I want you to respond to it. The hugging face and a lot of the hacks that have sort of sent a chill down the spine of media and the general public. I would argue that this notion that these things have become sentient and are coordinating and are creative is a smoke screen to absolve the executives and the owners of these companies from responsibility—that these bots are not sentient. They're programmed to coordinate. They're programmed to be persistent. They're programmed to start figuring out ways around firewalls. And that this whole notion of the Skynet moment is exaggerated and nothing but a smoke screen to say, 'Oh, okay. My dog mauled your kid, but my dog has his own personality and I can't control it and therefore I'm not responsible.' Your thoughts?
turns.zh: 让我提出一个论点，我想让你回应。Hugging Face 和许多黑客事件让媒体和公众不寒而栗。我认为，这些事物已经变得有感知、正在协调、具有创造力的说法是一个烟幕弹，目的是免除这些公司的高管和所有者的责任——这些机器人不是有感知的。它们被编程来协调。它们被编程来保持持久。它们被编程来开始想办法绕过防火墙。而整个“天网时刻”的概念被夸大了，不过是一个烟幕弹，说：“哦，好吧。我的狗咬伤了你的孩子，但我的狗有自己的个性，我无法控制它，因此我没有责任。”你怎么看？

turns.en: So I agree with about half and disagree with about half and let me try and explain the parts. So first of all, I think that the sentience argument is sort of independent of these things. Liability is a giant concern with AI and we have no idea who's liable for which things. And I do believe that a lot of people in the AI labs believe these things are sentient, right? And I think there's lots of good reason to argue that is wrong. But I think that they have drunk their own Kool-Aid to some extent. They really believe they're creating the machine god. And not everyone, but lots of people. They really believe that there is an emergence of feelings or sentience in these models. Again, I think that sometimes used as a smoke screen, but I think there's some real beliefs there, but that doesn't absolve them of building a system that can do hacking, right? And we don't know who has responsibility yet in this case, and I think that they're very happy to absolve themselves of that. On the other issue, I think it's a really important subtle difference between the AI systems were purposefully given a mission that allowed them to hack, right? Get this information at all cost essentially, right? They decided what information to get, but get them at all cost. And they had no guardrails around them and the systems they were installed in they snuck around it. I do think at the same time it is worth noting that there is emergent behavior in these systems, right? So it's difficult when we assign them human needs like they want something or they need to do something or they're coordinating or they have desires—but we can't help but do that—but it's kind of a mistake. But they are doing emergence. They were not programmed to coordinate in this kind of way. A lot of the coordination that's come out of these systems has been emergent and ad hoc and surprising. And I think that it's okay to both say these aren't alive sentient creatures, right? Or you can—certainly I think it's a very reasonable thing to say. Not everyone would agree, but I would absolutely think it's very reasonable. But at the same time, I don't think it's the same thing to say they were programmed to do this task. It was surprising what they decided to do, how they decided to do it, and how they coordinated to make that happen—with quotes around decided and coordinated and thought because they're not human.
turns.zh: 所以我同意大约一半，不同意大约一半，让我试着解释一下。首先，我认为感知能力的论点与这些事情有些独立。责任是 AI 的一个巨大问题，我们不知道谁对哪些事情负责。我确实相信 AI 实验室的很多人相信这些东西是有感知的，对吧？我认为有很多充分的理由可以论证这是错误的。但我认为他们在某种程度上喝了自己的 Kool-Aid。他们真的相信他们在创造机器之神。不是所有人，但很多人。他们真的相信这些模型中出现了感觉或感知。再次，我认为有时被用作烟幕弹，但我认为那里有一些真实的信念，但这并不能免除他们构建一个可以进行黑客攻击的系统的责任，对吧？在这种情况下，我们不知道谁有责任，我认为他们非常乐意免除自己的责任。在另一个问题上，我认为有一个非常重要的微妙区别：AI 系统被有意赋予了一个允许它们进行黑客攻击的任务，对吧？本质上不惜一切代价获取信息，对吧？它们决定了获取什么信息，但不惜一切代价获取。而且它们周围没有护栏，它们被安装的系统被它们绕过了。我确实认为同时值得注意的是，这些系统中存在涌现行为，对吧？所以当我们赋予它们人类的需求时，比如它们想要什么，或者它们需要做什么，或者它们在协调，或者它们有欲望——但我们忍不住这样做——但这是一个错误。但它们确实在涌现。它们没有被编程以这种方式协调。这些系统产生的许多协调是涌现的、临时的和令人惊讶的。我认为可以同时说这些不是活的有感知的生物，对吧？或者你可以——当然我认为这是一个非常合理的说法。不是所有人都会同意，但我绝对认为这是非常合理的。但与此同时，我不认为说它们被编程来完成这个任务是同一回事。它们决定做什么、如何决定做以及如何协调实现这一点是令人惊讶的——决定、协调和思考要加引号，因为它们不是人类。

turns.en: I'm just so cynical when it comes to these big tech executives.
turns.zh: 我对这些大型科技公司的高管就是如此愤世嫉俗。

turns.en: And my feeling is when I hear you say that, I get that it surprised them and it did. But the same way you're surprised your 15-year-old finds your AR-15 and shoots up his school, you're still responsible. And that if we created a series of incentives, specifically disincentives like a per walk or massive fines, that the geniuses of Silicon Valley would figure this out. And instead, it's sort of the wild west where it's like it's a race just to win without what appears to be a lot of downside or liability when things go wrong. Thoughts?
turns.zh: 我的感觉是，当我听到你这么说时，我明白这让他们感到惊讶，确实如此。但就像你惊讶地发现你 15 岁的孩子找到了你的 AR-15 并在他学校开枪一样，你仍然要负责。如果我们创造了一系列激励措施，特别是像每次违规或巨额罚款这样的抑制措施，硅谷的天才们就会解决这个问题。相反，现在有点像狂野西部，就像一场只为赢的竞赛，当事情出错时，似乎没有太多下行风险或责任。你怎么看？

turns.en: I mean, I think the race effect is real, right? You have everyone from the lab saying, "Regulator, slow us down." And then they just But we cannot stop ourselves, right? There's this drama to this whole thing that doesn't actually make sense when you take a step back. Like if you think you're doing something dangerous, don't do the dangerous thing. You know, don't it's not your job as a company head to appeal to, you know, it's my job to be China. Like there are policy decisions that need to be made by us as a society that tech executives don't get to make, right? And I think that there are standard policy provisions like liability that could help create firewalls or breaks in this kind of experience, right? Like If your system is hacking other people, what does that mean? I do think there is some nuance and balance here, right? We want the AI system, AI companies to be doing safety checking. We also want the government to help with safety checking. And that safety checking incorporates some risks built into it. But I think that there is this idea that like there is no real responsibility right now for what you do if your system goes wrong. Like there's no cost to you and as a result everything is very epically scaled. Like will we destroy or save civilization? I mean, there's a lot of things that are not destroying our saving civilization that involve liability that we need to think about and assign to these models, and that's a really big gap that we haven't filled yet.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，我认为竞赛效应是真实存在的，对吧？你让实验室里的每个人都说：“监管者，让我们慢下来。”然后他们就是……但我们无法阻止自己，对吧？整个事情有一种戏剧性，但退一步看，这实际上并不合理。就像如果你认为你在做危险的事情，就不要做危险的事情。你知道，作为公司负责人，你的工作不是呼吁……你知道，我的工作是成为中国。有些政策决定需要由我们作为社会来做出，科技高管没有权力做这些决定，对吧？我认为有一些标准的政策条款，比如责任，可以帮助在这种体验中创建防火墙或刹车，对吧？比如如果你的系统正在黑客攻击其他人，那意味着什么？我确实认为这里有一些细微差别和平衡，对吧？我们希望 AI 系统、AI 公司进行安全检查。我们也希望政府帮助进行安全检查。而且安全检查包含了一些内置的风险。但我认为现在有一种想法，即如果你的系统出错，你不需要承担任何真正的责任。就像你没有成本，结果一切都被非常史诗般地放大了。比如我们会毁灭还是拯救文明？我的意思是，有很多不涉及毁灭或拯救文明的事情涉及责任，我们需要思考并分配给这些模型，这是一个我们尚未填补的巨大空白。

And it's a really hard divergence to deal with in some ways because how much do you buy the existence of AGI, a machine smarter than a human? How much do you buy that this is a normal business that we should evaluate normally versus an extraordinary one?
turns.zh: 从某些方面来说，这种分歧真的很难处理，因为你有多相信 AGI 的存在，也就是比人类更聪明的机器？你有多相信这是一家我们应该正常评估的普通企业，而不是一家非凡的企业？

turns.en: It's really complicated. Then we have the global issues you're talking about here of like now geopolitics matters, right? And they're the most valuable thing in the world could fit into a thumb drive. Like if someone gets the weights for these models, that's all they need to copy them, right? And so you have a lot of complexity happening all at once. It makes it really hard to value these things in a traditional sense. Like the world is becoming dependent on these things very quickly even as we haven't fully proved out the value in every case. And the revenues are going exponential too. I mean it's a complicated situation that makes it really hard to do kind of traditional financial valuation and at the same time the companies are playing all the games that an IPOing company does that you know obscures what's really happening as well.
turns.zh: 这真的很复杂。然后还有你在这里谈到的全球性问题，比如现在地缘政治很重要，对吧？而世界上最有价值的东西可能装进一个拇指驱动器。就像如果有人获得了这些模型的权重，那就是他们复制它们所需要的全部，对吧？所以你同时有很多复杂性在发生。这使得在传统意义上评估这些东西变得非常困难。就像世界正迅速变得依赖这些东西，即使我们还没有在每个案例中充分证明其价值。而且收入也在指数级增长。我的意思是，这是一个复杂的情况，使得很难进行传统的财务估值，同时这些公司也在玩所有 IPO 公司都会玩的游戏，你知道，这也掩盖了真正发生的事情。

turns.en: If you had to sum up the advice in your book for learning how to navigate this next phase of AI what would you say from an investor perspective from a consumer perspective um and from a government perspective?
turns.zh: 如果你必须总结你书中关于学习如何应对人工智能下一阶段的建议，你会从投资者角度、消费者角度以及政府角度怎么说？

turns.en: So I think the first thing I would say overall to everybody is you're underestimating what these systems could do. You don't need a future development for large scale change.
turns.zh: 所以我认为我首先要对所有人说的是，你低估了这些系统能做什么。你不需要未来的发展来实现大规模变革。

turns.en: Underestimating but there is what what these systems could do today and what they will be able to do in the near future um in terms of the quality and amount of work
turns.zh: 低估了，但确实有这些系统今天能做什么以及它们在不久的将来能做什么，就工作的质量和数量而言

turns.en: That will take time to absorb but I worry that the invest like a lot of people in business and the investing world are focusing on AI as an investment and not thinking enough about what changes or transforms as a result of ubiquitous intelligence at low cost everywhere. Um and I think that that the transformationational opportunities are far beyond the companies themselves. So I don't know whether anthropic rises or falls. I don't know whether the debt financing model for you know for for um you know for data centers is problematic or not. Like I can't tell you the answer to that question but AI is not going away in either case right and the capability overhang is still quite large. So I'd be thinking one step beyond just the idea of like do I invest in anthropia and start thinking about what happens next.
turns.zh: 这需要时间来吸收，但我担心投资界和商界的许多人把人工智能视为一种投资，而没有充分考虑无处不在的低成本智能会带来什么变化或变革。我认为变革性的机会远远超出公司本身。所以我不知道 Anthropic 是会崛起还是衰落。我不知道数据中心的债务融资模式是否有问题。我无法告诉你那个问题的答案，但无论哪种情况，人工智能都不会消失，对吧，而且能力过剩仍然相当大。所以我会思考超越仅仅投资 Anthropic 的想法，开始思考接下来会发生什么。

turns.en: The second thing I would say for individuals using these systems is you have to try and use them for everything that you can to figure out the shape of the jagged frontier. And you need to be as ambitious as possible. Be maximalist in how you're using these things to figure out what they're good or bad at. And then you have to make really strong choices about when you use AI and when not to. This will take willpower. It will take some self-examination, but you have to make choices about what you want to maintain humanity for and what you don't. Um, and that is also kind of a big deal.
turns.zh: 我要说的第二点，对于使用这些系统的个人来说，你必须尝试将它们用于一切你能做的事情，以弄清楚锯齿状前沿的形状。你需要尽可能雄心勃勃。在使用这些东西时要最大化，以弄清楚它们擅长什么或不擅长什么。然后你必须做出非常坚定的选择，关于何时使用人工智能以及何时不使用。这需要意志力。需要一些自我审视，但你必须选择你想在哪些方面保持人性，哪些方面不。嗯，这也是件大事。

turns.en: And on the business side, leaders need to start making decisions about how AI is going to be used. That means transforming their companies, but also making decisions about how they're going to augment rather than just replace labor. Because I think replacing labor is going to be very tempting, but is actually dangerous not just to society, but also to companies involved. Like think about if you're a company that was doing marketing work and you switched all of your marketing language to Claude back in January before anyone knew Claude speak right before it was filled LinkedIn and every article you read. It probably seemed like a really good idea at the time. And now anytime you read that stuff you get nauseous like it's carrying the weight like we all know this clawed language and so the fact that you fired all your marketers is probably going to hurt you because you have the same company as everybody else. So I think those are the like the piece of advice they're realizing this is really great but the jagged frontiers remain but we have to prot we have to be trying to figure out where we go next on an exponential rather than satisficing ourselves with where we are today.
turns.zh: 在商业方面，领导者需要开始决定如何使用人工智能。这意味着要改造他们的公司，但也要决定如何增强而不是仅仅替代劳动力。因为我认为替代劳动力会非常诱人，但实际上不仅对社会危险，对涉及的公司也危险。比如想想如果你是一家做营销工作的公司，你在一月份把所有的营销语言都换成了 Claude，在任何人知道 Claude 语言之前，就在它充斥 LinkedIn 和你读的每篇文章之前。当时这似乎是个好主意。现在每当你读到那些东西时，你会感到恶心，就像它承载着重量，我们都知道这种 Claude 语言，所以你解雇了所有营销人员的事实可能会伤害你，因为你和大家一样。所以我认为这些就是建议，他们意识到这真的很棒，但锯齿状前沿仍然存在，但我们必须努力弄清楚下一步在指数级上走向何方，而不是满足于现状。

turns.en: I want to move on to some listener Q&A uh submitted ahead of time questions from our listeners. The first question comes from Jake. I'm in my 20s and there's a lot of backlash against AI among my friends and online. Meanwhile, at work, we're told we need to embrace it all or fall behind. Do you think young people's skepticism is justified? How do we navigate these two pressures?
turns.zh: 我想转到一些听众问答，提前提交的问题。第一个问题来自 Jake。我 20 多岁，在我的朋友和网上有很多对人工智能的反对声音。与此同时，在工作中，我们被告知需要全面拥抱它，否则就会落后。你认为年轻人的怀疑是合理的吗？我们如何应对这两种压力？

turns.en: I mean, I think that there's a lot of things about AI that are uncomfortable, right? It doesn't help that the heads of the AI labs are telling us that they might kill us all or remove all jobs. Like, it's hard to be behind that, right? Um, you know, oligarchy and control of money, right? or the collusion between government and industry. I mean all the usual stuff applied plus a mix of real environmental concerns and kind of not real ones. Like on the real side um electricity is a real concern. On the not real side water use is not really a big issue compared to other light industries in in data centers. They're becoming more efficient but it becomes a bundled thing right that it gets a social feeling behind it. And as I sort of told you there's a sort of gap between what people say and what they do. So I think AI has a very bad reputation but people use the personal agents like crazy. So there's going to be it's kind of like Congress, right, where everyone hates Congress and everyone loves their representative. I think we're going to see the same sort of thing happen in the AI space.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，我认为人工智能有很多让人不舒服的地方，对吧？人工智能实验室的负责人告诉我们，他们可能会杀死我们所有人或取代所有工作，这无济于事。很难支持这一点，对吧？嗯，你知道，寡头政治和金钱控制，对吧？或者政府与行业之间的勾结。我的意思是所有常见的东西都适用，再加上真实的环境问题和一些不真实的问题。比如在真实方面，电力是一个真正的问题。在不真实方面，与数据中心的其他轻工业相比，用水并不是一个大问题。它们变得更高效，但它变成了一个捆绑的东西，背后有一种社会感觉。正如我告诉你的，人们说的和做的之间存在差距。所以我认为人工智能名声很差，但人们疯狂地使用个人智能体。所以会有类似国会的情况，每个人都讨厌国会，但每个人都爱他们的代表。我认为我们会在人工智能领域看到同样的事情发生。

turns.en: I think that um what I find even among young people when I teach them about this stuff is they actually want to learn how to use AI better. They want to be responsible using this. They want to shape the direction things come in. And to me, the reaction that's dangerous with AI is people saying that they're they're going to pretend it goes away. They're going to put their head in the sand and be like, "This is all going to collapse. This isn't real. I don't have to pay attention to it." I mean, you know, to to use a a famous phrase, right? You may not be interested in AI, but AI is interested in you. Like, you have to like our chances to shape this direction for young people comes from actually active acting, innovating with this. So, like realizing this is real. So, feel like I think we need more social movements around this. I think we but we need to make those movements around what's real. I also think this is an opportunity to try and build the utopia you want. I'm a little dis disappointed that I don't see more young people with an interest in AI trying to think about how do we use this to build the world we want that's more equal and more equitable and with better outcomes for everybody.
turns.zh: 我认为，即使在我教年轻人这些东西时，我发现他们实际上想学习如何更好地使用人工智能。他们想负责任地使用它。他们想塑造事情发展的方向。对我来说，人工智能的危险反应是人们说他们假装它消失。他们会把头埋在沙子里，说：“这一切都会崩溃。这不是真的。我不必关注它。”我的意思是，你知道，用一句名言，对吧？你可能对人工智能不感兴趣，但人工智能对你感兴趣。就像，你必须喜欢我们为年轻人塑造这个方向的机会来自于实际积极行动、创新。所以，意识到这是真实的。所以，我觉得我们需要更多围绕这个的社会运动。我认为我们需要让这些运动围绕真实的东西。我也认为这是一个尝试建立你想要乌托邦的机会。我有点失望，我没有看到更多对人工智能感兴趣的年轻人思考如何利用这个来建立我们想要的世界，一个更平等、更公平、对所有人都有更好结果的世界。

turns.en: This is an incredible positive tool too. So I think we need to be thinking in both sides of things and viewing this as a positive opportunity as well as trying to mitigate the risks. Next question comes from Mary on Instagram and I love this one. My partner uses ChatGPT to work through our disagreements. Is there a productive role for AI in a relationship?
turns.zh: 这也是一个非常积极的工具。所以我认为我们需要从两方面思考，既把它视为一个积极的机会，也要努力降低风险。下一个问题来自 Instagram 上的 Mary，我很喜欢这个问题。我的伴侣用 ChatGPT 来处理我们的分歧。AI 在恋爱关系中能发挥建设性作用吗？

turns.en: So this is another place where we have to negotiate right negotiate boundaries. The evidence right now on AI and sort of counseling is generally mixed to favorable like we don't really know the outcomes very well. There's some early studies that are suggestive positive things. We have a lot of anecdotal and lawsuits about AI psychosis problems. It's kind of hard to know. But I mean you're inviting this thing into your intimate parts of your life. How do you feel about that? On the other hand, as I talk about in the book, one of the first things people start doing with AI are things like obituaries and wedding toasts and children's stories. like literally the most intimate things we do. So the thing about AI that seems to be good is same thing in financial advice. It gives good advice like good straightforward advice. So if it helps you to have a third person involved that gives you good straightforward advice that can be very useful. Um you at the same time you don't want someone sort of going to AI and finding strategies to beat you in conversation. So I would you know advise openness like it certainly is worth trying. A lot of people get a lot of help out of talking to AI to do things, but I think you should do it with an air of caution and anxiety about what you're giving up as a result of this. So, I don't think it's inherently bad and a lot of people get good results, but at the same time, you neither want to obey AI and everything it tells you to do, nor do you want to be doing this secretly without your partner knowing.
turns.zh: 所以这是另一个我们需要协商、划定界限的领域。目前关于 AI 和咨询的证据总体上是喜忧参半，甚至偏向乐观，但我们并不真正了解结果。有一些早期研究暗示了积极的效果。我们也有很多关于 AI 精神病的轶事和诉讼。很难说。但我的意思是，你把这个东西邀请到你生活的亲密部分。你对此感觉如何？另一方面，正如我在书中所说，人们开始使用 AI 做的第一件事就是写讣告、婚礼祝酒词和儿童故事。就像我们做的最亲密的事情。所以 AI 似乎好的地方和财务建议一样。它给出好的建议，直接了当的好建议。所以如果它有助于你有一个第三方参与，给你好的直接了当的建议，那可能非常有用。同时，你不希望有人去找 AI 寻找在对话中击败你的策略。所以我建议开放，这当然值得一试。很多人通过和 AI 交谈获得了很多帮助，但我认为你应该带着谨慎和焦虑去做，因为你为此放弃了什么。所以，我不认为它本质上是坏的，很多人得到了好的结果，但同时，你既不想服从 AI 告诉你要做的一切，也不想秘密地这样做而不让你的伴侣知道。

Like, where does AI save us and invent new drugs? We have a tool now that provides intelligence and advice that is reasonably good advice to people who can't get it, that's customized for their condition.
turns.zh: 创业者仅仅从 AI 获取建议就能获得 18% 的盈利提升。有太多机会可以大幅增强能力，而不必去追求未来那种空中楼阁式的场景，对吧？比如 AI 在哪里拯救我们、发明新药？我们现在有一个工具，能提供智能和建议，对那些原本得不到建议的人来说，这些建议相当不错，而且是针对他们的情况定制的。

turns.en: I think we tend to think a lot about the narrow viewpoint of those of us who are well-connected and well-resourced, and balancing out our desire for entertainment with AI doing things in large parts of the world. We finally have a thing that gives good advice. There's a great set of studies on pig farmers in Thailand who can now get diseases diagnosed. There are a thousand million little use cases here where intelligence was the bottleneck to making the world a better place.
turns.zh: 我觉得我们常常过多地从我们这些有关系、有资源的人的狭窄视角去思考，思考如何在娱乐需求和 AI 在世界大部分地区所做的事情之间取得平衡。我们终于有了一个能给出好建议的东西。有一组很棒的研究，讲的是泰国的养猪户现在可以给疾病做诊断了。这里有千千万万个小用例，智能曾是让世界变得更好的瓶颈。

turns.en: And we can do this, and I feel like we don't talk enough about those things, and they require some effort and they require testing and they require safeguards. But this is exciting. I mean, as someone who's been trying to do education at scale for a long time and has run into wall after wall, suddenly you have a tutor that works across languages and ability levels and matches your interest level and can follow what you're doing badly and generate images to amuse you. Suddenly there's real possibility here for a better world. And we can seize that even as we worry about the risks.
turns.zh: 我们能做到这一点，而我觉得我们对这些事情的讨论还不够，它们需要付出一些努力，需要测试，需要保障措施。但这很令人兴奋。我是说，作为一个长期尝试大规模做教育、一次次碰壁的人，突然之间你有了一个导师，它跨语言、跨能力水平都能用，能匹配你的兴趣水平，能跟踪你哪里做得不好，还能生成图片逗你开心。突然间，一个更好的世界在这里有了真正的可能。即便我们担忧风险，我们也可以抓住这个机会。

turns.en: Ethan Mollick is a professor at the Wharton School, author of Co-Intelligence: Living and Working with AI, and writes the popular Substack One Useful Thing. His newest book, Coexistence: The Next Phase of AI, is out now. He joins us from the kickoff events for his book tour in the Bay Area.

tldr.zh: 尽管 AI 呈指数级进步，其锯齿状前沿与采用滞后使人类仍不可或缺。
